narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 78% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission, this probability led to your application being rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (compared to an average of roughly the middle of the class among accepted students) signaled that your performance placed you well behind most successful applicants. Your LSAT score was the next most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure; a score of 26 is substantially below the average of 37 seen among those who were admitted. These two elements together outweighed the one positive signal in your profile: your undergraduate GPA of 3.10, which slightly lowered the predicted risk of failure because it was reasonably close to the 3.23 average of accepted students.

Your first-year ranking (bottom decile versus an average around 6) and family income level played smaller roles and were not decisive. The model did not consider your gender or race.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to bring your score closer to the typical range of admitted students. Stronger results in these areas would significantly lower your predicted risk on future applications. (218 words)
